p: Sam Okafor has run the Halcyon for twenty two months, and the target burn is February 18, 2063.
When Greaves aired AR 2207's closure record, Sam had already called the crew, Frances, Bea, Hana, and the board, and he gave Greaves the facts on the record.
The readiness board will choose in December between flying the valve with a software workaround and replacing it by spacewalk, and the workaround's ground runs are its evidence.
A partner government pulled sixteen million dollars after an election, and launch 3, with the Breather and its lander, flies in November.
Then Wendell collapsed at the console during a night ground run, and though he's all right, he says this is his last campaign: he'll see it to December, and then he's done.
Wendell Price. Test conductor, seventy one.
Arlo Dunn. The stand's night technician, thirty one, from Limon.
Ruth Calder. On the readiness board, and the Petrel's flight director.
Corinne Mathers. Leads the new merged Integration and Test team of sixty seven.
Yusra Haddad. Halcyon's commander, and now the product owner of the flight software backlog.
Quinn Abernathy. The scheduler, fast becoming Sam's right hand.
Imogen Hale. Director of the Ares Relief Authority, which owns the mission and pays for it.
Dr. Anjali Rao. The doctor on Halcyon's crew.
Delphine Varga. Mission manager at Coquina Launch Services, which owns the rockets for all three launches.
Chiamaka Okonkwo. Breather operations lead on Ares Station.
Ada Okafor. Sam's daughter on Ares Station.
New in this chapter: Lorna Whitcombe, Ilse Brandvold and Mateo Echeverría.

Friday, November 10. 4:15 AM. The chair by the bed was the kind hospitals buy because it folds out, and it didn't fold out, and Sam had stopped trying at three. Wendell was asleep with his mouth open and his hearing protection still around his neck. A nurse had tried to take it off him at midnight. He'd woken up long enough to say no.

His canvas jacket was on the hook behind the door. The pockets were worn through at the corners, and one of them had a pencil in it, and a run sheet from the blockhouse folded in quarters. Sam unfolded it standing up.

WORKAROUND GROUND RUN THU NOV 9 2062 W. PRICE, TC. SOAK 1 START 1700. SOAK 2 START 2030.. CONDITIONING CYCLE BEFORE EACH CLOSE. MOIV-2 CLOSED AT CUTOFF.. SOAK 1. CYCLE 1 OK. 2 OK. 3 RIPPLE 2 MS AFTER LIFT, UNDER LIMIT. 4 OK. 5 OK. 6 OK.. SOAK 2. CYCLE 7 OK. 8 OK. 9 RIPPLE 2 MS AFTER LIFT, UNDER LIMIT.. 10

Cycle nine had a tick beside it, in pencil, pressed hard enough to dent the paper. Cycle ten had a number and nothing after it. Sam folded the sheet back along its creases and put it where it had been.
At 4:40 Wendell opened his eyes and looked at the ceiling and said, without turning his head, The shoebox is in the truck. Truck's at the stand.
Bring the truck. Leave the box in it. They're mine. Then he went back to sleep, as if that had been the only thing on his list.

Arlo met Sam at the stand gate at 5:30 with two coffees, and they drove out together on the gravel in the dark. Wendell's truck was where he'd left it, nose to the blockhouse wall, with the window down an inch the way he always left it so the cab wouldn't fog. The shoebox was on the passenger seat with its rubber bands on, and a thermos on top of it like a paperweight. Sam drove it back to Byers and put the keys under the mat and didn't open the box.

On the way back he came past the high bay. The countdown clock over the doors said 100. It had said three figures since the day he got the job, and he hadn't thought about what it would look like when it didn't.

What he did think about, all the way in on I-70 with the sun coming up behind him, was the thing Wendell had stood up at 10:52 to look at, the second before he fell. Nobody knew what it was. Wendell knew. It was in his head with everything else, the ripples and the frost and the sound a seat made when it was lying, and his head had just spent four hours on a monitor in Aurora.

Saturday, November 11. There was an envelope in the mailbox, in green ink, postmarked Golden, and it said S. OKAFOR. Inside it, smaller, folded in half, was another one, and it said, on the front, FOR W. IF HE WANTS IT.

Monday, November 13. 6:05 AM. Wendell's truck was at the stand gate when Sam got there, with the engine off and the window down its inch. Wendell was in the blockhouse in his canvas jacket, pouring coffee from the thermos, as if Thursday had been somebody else's.

He had a sheet from the hospital folded in quarters in his shirt pocket, and he handed it over without being asked, which was how Sam knew he'd decided to fight. Discharged Friday afternoon. Low blood pressure, a medication to stop, a cardiology appointment in December. Under restrictions, in a doctor's handwriting: No night work. No working alone. No more than five hours a day, three days a week. Light duty until cleared.

Light duty's a console, Wendell said. I sit in a chair. Tuesday night's run is cycles eleven to twenty, after a long soak, on the lot valve. That's the run the board's going to read in December. I'd like to be the one who reads it first.

Corinne was in the doorway with her legal pad. Tallgrass's occupational health nurse had called her at seven on Friday: nobody went back on a hazardous operation after an event like that without a fitness for duty review, and the stand at night, with cryogens on it, was a hazardous operation. Garrett had texted Sam at 9:40 on Saturday night. Board's evidence is his read. Get him back on nights. Hana had written something shorter on Sunday. I'd rather lose the run than lose him.

Arlo was at the far bench with his back to all of them, sorting connectors. He'd made the call from the stand on Thursday night and been in the blockhouse door a minute later, and he'd knelt on the floor beside Quinn until the ambulance came.
Around the site, since Friday, the story had gone four ways. It was his heart. It was a stroke. He was retiring. He'd been let go.

He takes Wendell out to the truck, where there's nobody, and asks him what he wants. It takes Wendell a while. I want somebody to read that trace who knows what they're looking at. Then I want to go home. So they build it around that. The nurse clears him on Tuesday for days, inside the doctor's hours. Tuesday's run moves to Wednesday at ten in the morning, with the soak started at four by Arlo and a second tech. Wendell sits beside the console and Arlo sits at it. At the huddle Sam says one sentence about it: Wendell was ill on Thursday, he's back on days, and his health is his business. The four stories stop by Friday.
Tuesday, November 14. 7:30 AM. Wendell was in the big room at seven thirty because seven thirty was inside his five hours. He'd brought the thermos.

Everybody wanted something from him, and everybody had written it down. Garrett's email had come in at 6:02 with a subject line in capitals. KNOWLEDGE CAPTURE. GET IT ALL. EVERY PAGE, EVERY RUN, EVERY STORY. Hana wanted his read of every cycle three since 2059, for the root cause team. Commander Haddad, on the screen from Houston, wanted to know what she'd be looking at on her display at cutoff, and what it would mean. Lorna Whitcombe, who ran the ARA's flight operations and would fly Halcyon after it left, wanted the console calls. Quinn wanted the propulsion poll.

Rafa had a suggestion, and a demo. The ARA had cleared an interview assistant for program use in the spring: you talked, it asked follow up questions, it wrote everything into a searchable record. Quinn watched the demo and wrote SEARCH on her pad in capitals and underlined it.

Wendell listened to all of it. Then he said, to the table, I've got thirty one days and the doctor says I can use about seventy five hours of them. You can have all of it. You can't have all of it by December.

It takes the morning, with Wendell and Quinn at the whiteboard and everybody else sent out. They work backward from the dates. December 14, the board picks between the workaround and the spacewalk. January 9, the crew launches. February 18, the burn. Then they ask what each of those needs from Wendell's head, and in whose head it has to be by then. It comes to seven lines. Running a cold soak campaign and reading cycle three live: Arlo, by December 15. Telling a seat from ice from a lying sensor on a trace: the crew, Hana, and Lorna's controllers, by January 9. The propulsion poll: Quinn. His read of every cycle three since 2059: Hana's root cause team, before the board. The rest, the Petrel's campaigns and nearly fifty years of notebooks, goes in a column headed LATER, OR NEVER, in Wendell's own hand.

Wednesday, November 15. 10:00 AM. The run was on at the stand, cycles eleven to twenty after a long soak, with Arlo at the console and Wendell in the chair beside it with a headset on. Sam watched from the back of the blockhouse with Quinn.

Halfway through, on the third cycle after the soak, Wendell said, There, and Arlo Dunn, the stand tech learning his console, said, Where? and Wendell didn't answer, because by the time he could have, it was over. The trace on the screen looked like every other trace. Quinn wrote down the time.

Quinn's seven lines from Tuesday were taped to the blockhouse wall above the coffee can. The question now was how. Garrett's office had sent a template, a procedure package, forty headings long. Commander Haddad had asked for the crew to be in the room. Ilse Brandvold, her pilot, had asked a better question in an email Sam read twice: When he says there, what does he see that we don't? Can he teach us to see it, or only to follow the steps?
Wendell had his hours. Five a day, three days a week, until the fifteenth of December.

They build it from his hours. Two mornings a week Arlo sits the console on live runs and Wendell sits beside him, two headsets on the same channel, and Wendell says there out loud before it's over, every time, and then they replay it until Arlo hears it too. Quinn sits the poll with him. Twice the crew comes up from Houston to the sim bay, and Wendell stands behind Haddad and Brandvold with a printout of real traces and makes them call each one. Everything's recorded, with his say, and after every session Quinn writes up what came out of it in one page and Wendell crosses out what's wrong. By the second week there's a sentence on the whiteboard in his capitals: IF POSITION WIGGLES AND PRESSURE DOESN'T, BELIEVE THE PRESSURE. Brandvold writes it on her kneeboard card.

Sunday, November 19. 2:00 PM. Byers. Wendell's kitchen had one window and it faced the grain elevator, and he'd put the table under it so he could see the weather coming. Sam had brought the small green envelope. Quinn had brought the recorder, for the sessions Wendell had said yes to, and a folder from Tallgrass legal.
Wendell read Ruth's page with his reading glasses pushed down his nose and his lips moving a little. He read it twice. He stopped at the thirteen forty one line for a long time.
She wrote it down, he said. I always figured she'd thrown that day out. He folded the page along its old crease and put it in his shirt pocket, behind the doctor's note.

Then he talked, for forty minutes, without anybody asking. About frost. The thermocouple sat on the flange, he said, and the flange lagged, so it told you what the valve had been an hour ago. The frost line on the camera told you now. When the frost had climbed past the second bolt on the body, the seat was cold where it counted, and that was the only cycle worth watching. About the sound. A good close was one knock in the headset. A bad one had a shoulder on it, a softer knock a couple of milliseconds behind, and you heard the shoulder before the trace could draw it.
Quinn reached over and pressed the red button on the recorder, and Wendell stopped in the middle of a word and looked at it.

In the legal folder there was a form. KNOWLEDGE CAPTURE RELEASE. ALL NOTES, RECORDINGS, AND MATERIALS PROVIDED BECOME THE PROPERTY OF TALLGRASS AEROSPACE. Under it was a note from Garrett's office asking that the shoebox be scanned and kept in the company archive as program records. The shoebox was on the counter by the sink with its rubber bands on.
And there was the other thing, which Sam had in his pocket on a card in his own handwriting, copied from page ten: PROP ANSWERED FIRST. WENDELL. GO. HE TOOK A SECOND.

The legal folder goes back in Sam's bag, unopened, under a bag of jerky from the gas station in Bennett. Your house, your rules. You tell Quinn when it's on. You read what she writes and cross out what's wrong. The notebooks are yours. If you ever want copies somewhere, you say where. Wendell looks at him for a while. Then he reaches over and presses the red button himself and finishes the word he was in the middle of. In the car Quinn says he's going to let them scan the 2034 notebook. He told her so while Sam was in the bathroom. He said, she'd want it kept. He meant Ruth. Sam doesn't ask him about the second, then or later.

Monday, December 4. 8:00 AM. The high bay was empty for the first time since the summer of 2059. All three of Halcyon's modules had left it, and the floor where they'd stood was swept, and the overhead cranes were parked at the far end with their hooks up, like birds on a wire. The last of the three launches had flown in November. Corinne's people were still on the payroll, sixty seven of them, and most of them had nothing left to build.

She had the plan on her legal pad, copied from the merger's resource plan in April, which had given every person a date. Thirty eight people released on Friday, December 15: some to Tallgrass's next program, some to the end of their contracts, eleven to jobs elsewhere that started the week after. Seventeen more on Friday, January 12, once the crew had launched. Twelve kept through Friday, February 23, the sustaining team for departure. She'd told all of them in April, in writing, and again in September.

Garrett's position was in an email with the subject line NOBODY LEAVES. Keep all sixty seven through departure. The ship was in orbit with a valve nobody understood, and he wasn't going to explain to anybody why the people who'd built it were working somewhere else.

Hale's office in Denver had sent the other position on Friday: the partner committee's answer on the sixteen million was still pending, and the program should cut every cost it could, starting with people it didn't need.

Lorna Whitcombe had sent a third, which was a list of five names from Corinne's team that flight operations wanted on call until the burn, for things only they knew about the stack: two of the propellant loading crew, the harness technician who'd found the revision on the MOIV-1 position sensor, and two people from the Breather's stowage.

Corinne walks the list with Lorna on Tuesday morning. Four of Lorna's five names are already in the twelve. The fifth, the harness technician, was due to go on January 12; Corinne asks her, and she agrees to stay through the burn for a retention payment Peg writes up the same day. Everyone else goes on their date. Each person gets a letter from Sam that says what they built, by name and by part, and the ones going to other programs get a call from him to their new manager. Garrett's email gets a two line answer with the resource plan attached. On the 15th, at the high bay door, Corinne shakes thirty eight hands.

Tuesday, December 5. 9:00 AM. The crew's training backlog lived on a board in the sim bay, because Haddad said a thing she could see across a room was a thing she'd actually do. It had grown. Every card on it was somebody's good idea.
Between now and quarantine on December 26 the crew had about a hundred and forty hours left that weren't already spoken for. The cards on the board asked for two hundred and three.

Some of it was obviously theirs. The workaround procedure for CR 62-311, both versions, depending on December 14. Rafa's new cutoff displays. Dr. Rao's own list, which was medical and short. Wendell's sessions, two more in the sim bay, with real traces. Some of it was less obviously theirs. Hale's office had asked for an eight hour media block, for interviews from orbit. Garrett's comms office had asked for a four hour session on the Petrel, with Wendell, for a documentary. Two partners had each sent a cultural briefing.
Mateo Echeverría, the flight engineer, had a card of his own: The whole stage. Every valve. From the drawings. It was sixty hours on its own.
Commander Haddad stood in front of the board with her arms folded. I want all of it. I'm going to live on Mars. I'll have time to read there. I don't have time here.

They take the cards down one at a time, all two hundred and three hours of them, and Haddad asks each card the same thing out loud, the way a customs officer would: in flight, what do we do with you, and when? If there's an answer, the card stays, broken down to the task. If the answer is on Mars, it goes in a cardboard box Quinn labels CRUISE in marker. Two hundred days is a lot of reading time. No answer, and it goes back to whoever sent it, with a sticky note from Quinn. The media block becomes one hour. The documentary goes back to Garrett. Echeverría's sixty hours become eight, on the valves he'd actually touch, and the drawings go into the cruise box. The board comes to 131 hours, nine under. Haddad initials the bottom corner with a marker. Now it's mine.

Wednesday, December 6. 10:00 AM. Flight control at Watkins was a low building with a wind sock, and the wind sock was straight out. Lorna Whitcombe met Sam at the door with two coffees and the face of someone who'd been handed a lot of ships.

She'd flown four cargo landers to the Moon's south pole for the ARA, and one of them had landed on its side and kept working, and she had a photograph of it on her console. Her twelve controllers would fly Halcyon from the minute the program let go of it until it reached Mars, and then support the crew on the ground there. They'd sat in on every sim since August. They'd never owned anything on it.

The plan said the hand off was at departure plus twenty four hours, on February 19, after the burn and the first checkout. It didn't say much else. Garrett wanted the hand off at cutoff, the minute the burn ended, so Tallgrass's name would be on the burn and not on anything after it. Lorna Whitcombe, whose flight operations team would fly the ship after the hand off, had asked for the document package by January 1. I'll read it over the holidays and tell you what I think.

On the program's issue log there were nineteen open items. Most were small. One wasn't: I-62-117, MOIV-1 on orbit, root cause open, response to be chosen December 14. There was also the question of what the ship would do on its own if the crew couldn't act, which had never been anybody's option to fund.
Lorna put her coffee down. Tell me what I'm taking, Mr. Okafor. All of it. Including the parts you'd rather I found out about later.

They write it on her whiteboard that afternoon, in her words, and she signs it, and so does he. Nine conditions. Every controller certified on the Halcyon procedures in three integrated sims, two of them with failures Lorna picks and doesn't tell anyone about. The flight rules and the cutoff procedure, including the rule that a pressure reading outranks a position reading at cutoff, validated by her people in the sim, not by Tallgrass's. Every one of the nineteen open items listed with an owner on her side who has read it and accepted it, or a reason it stays with the program until the burn. I-62-117 stays where it belongs, with the board, which accepts the risk or doesn't on the 14th; Lorna's people own the procedure for living with whatever it decides. The hand off line itself, written as a time and a signature: departure plus twenty four hours. If any of these isn't true on the nineteenth, I won't take it, she says, and you won't want me to.

Friday, December 8. 7:30 AM. It had been Wendell's idea, which surprised nobody who knew him. On Thursday he'd picked twenty cycle threes out of the archive himself, from 2059 to last week, and stripped the dates and the run numbers off them. Six were real, by his reading: the seat doing the thing nobody could explain. The rest were ice, or the stand, or a sensor telling a lie. He'd sealed his answers in an envelope and given it to Hana.
Three people had read them blind. Arlo and Quinn had been beside him for three weeks of live runs. Haddad had had her two sessions in the sim bay and a printout she'd marked up on the plane.

The criteria were on the board, written on Wednesday with Lorna and Hana, before anybody had read a trace: miss no real event, make no more than two false calls, get at least ninety percent of the twenty right.

BLIND READS MOIV CYCLE 3 TRACES 20 ARCHIVED DEC 7 2062. KEY HELD BY H. IWASAKI. 6 REAL, 14 NOT.. ARLO DUNN: CALLED 6 REAL. 5 OF THE 6. 1 OF THE 14.. QUINN ABERNATHY: CALLED 9 REAL. ALL 6. 3 OF THE 14.. COMMANDER Y. HADDAD: CALLED 7 REAL. ALL 6. 1 OF THE 14.
Arlo had missed number eleven, from October 2059. He'd sat in front of the trace for a long time on Thursday, Hana said, and then called it ice.
Garrett had seen the sheet by eight. 90 percent is an A. Sign him off. Wendell's done on the 15th. Arlo hadn't said anything to anyone. He'd asked Hana for trace eleven back.

Wendell takes Arlo through trace eleven on Saturday morning, inside his five hours, at the kitchen table in Byers. It was the frost. The camera had been fogged on that run in 2059, and the thermocouple on the flange said cold, and the valve wasn't. You read it right off what you had. What you had was wrong. When the camera's out, you don't call it. That goes in the procedure too. On Tuesday Hana gives Arlo and Quinn twenty new traces. Arlo gets twenty. Quinn gets nineteen, one false call. On Wednesday morning, before the last run, Wendell signs Arlo off as test conductor on the back of the sheet, in pencil, and then again in ink when Corinne brings the form.
Saturday, December 9. 11:00 AM. Quinn came into the program room on a Saturday with two coffees and put one in front of Sam, which was the order things had always gone in between them.

She'd been named the countdown lead in November, in a memo from the program that the board had noted without comment. She'd run every rehearsal since. She ran them well. She sat down and put both hands flat on the table, which Sam had learned two years ago meant the news was bad, or that she was about to ask for something.

I've never run a real one, she said. I've run eleven rehearsals and I know the book cold. I don't know what it's like when it's the real thing and somebody's voice changes on the loop. Wendell does. He's leaving. Delphine's run forty two from her pad. And Ruth ran them for twenty two years. She looked at the coffee. I'm not asking for help. I'm asking who I should ask.
Garrett, who'd heard about the rehearsals from somebody, had already suggested that she shadow one of his vice presidents, who had once run a satellite launch for a different company.

He asks her first what she wants out of it. She's got a list, because she's Quinn, and it's on the back of a rehearsal script: hear a voice change on the loop and know what to ask; call a hold early and not apologize for it; run a poll when somebody takes a second. Delphine says yes on the phone before he's finished asking: an hour every Thursday until launch, on the loop with Quinn for two of the Cape rehearsals, and her number for the night of. Wendell says yes to one hour, on the poll, on the 11th. Ruth's name doesn't go on the list, and Quinn doesn't ask why; the board will judge the count. Garrett's vice president gets a polite note. On Thursday Delphine tells Quinn the first thing she ever learned about a countdown. The clock's the only thing in the room that isn't scared.

Monday, December 11. 8:15 AM. There was a new poster on the wall of flight control. Lorna's controllers had made it themselves over the weekend, and it was good, in the way of things made by tired people who like each other: Halcyon in silhouette, the wind sock, and in big letters, LAUNCH FEB 18. DELIVER THE BREATHER.

The engineering packet from Ares Station had come in overnight, from Chiamaka Okonkwo's Breather operations team, in the format they always used. Item four was a question. Who on Earth measures whether this worked, and when do they stop measuring? Our people are asking what success is. Most of them think it is breathing.

The families' newsletter that week had the countdown on its front page. Rafa's team had a sprint goal on their own whiteboard that ended at cutoff. The crew's training board ended at quarantine. Haddad's initials were on its bottom corner. Each picture was true, and each one stopped where somebody's job did.
Lorna had read item four before Sam had. They're right, you know. My poster ends at departure. My job doesn't end until they're breathing. Nobody's ever written down who decides that they are.

It takes two sessions, because the station is fifteen minutes away by light and answers a day later. Quinn writes the draft with Lorna, Haddad, and Rafa in one room, and sends it up in the packet, and Okonkwo's team sends it back marked up. What comes out is half a page. The benefit is the station's oxygen reserve rising instead of falling, measured on Ares Station, every sol, from the day the Breather starts until ninety sols after. The owner is someone on the station, named by the station before the crew leaves Earth, who reports to the board through the director's packet. Assumptions and risks underneath, in a list. Lorna's controllers take their poster down on Wednesday and put it back up with one line added under it in marker, in a controller's block capitals: AND THEN 90 SOLS OF AIR.
Tuesday, December 12. 5:40 AM. The kitchen in Aurora, with the coffee maker going. One way fifteen minutes and eight seconds.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4200. One way, 15 minutes 8 seconds. Margin, 259 days. Hi, Dad. Log fifty four. Sol 4200. I like a round number. Okonkwo says that's the most engineer thing about me. The crew's files came up in the packet. The parts we're allowed. Brandvold keeps bees in Montana and has a pilot's license for everything with wings. Echeverría fixed a desalination plant on a ship once, in a storm, and wrote a paper about it that I've now read twice. Dr. Rao has the shortest file and the longest list of what she's bringing, and Malik's already asked if any of it is chocolate. And Commander Haddad. Four kids. I'd been told that, but it's different in the file, where it's a line in a box. I picked her bunk. They let me. It's the one in C ring nearest the galley, which is the loud one, with the pumps under the floor and everybody going past at shift change. People think nobody wants it. I think somebody with four kids at home is going to want to hear people. If I'm wrong she can have mine. Something else. I've been keeping a log since the ration cut. Not this one. A station one, of what we got wrong. Okonkwo calls it the confession book. It's mostly hydroponics and two pages about the galley. I'll read you two, because I think you'll understand them. SOL 3561. RATION CUT. WE TOLD PEOPLE IT WAS TEMPORARY. IT WASN'T. DON'T SAY TEMPORARY. SOL 4013. STACK 3, CLAMP 2. I SAID THE LOOP WAS DRAINED. IT WASN'T. ASK HOW YOU KNOW. THEN ASK AGAIN. That's the whole method. Write the date, write what happened, write what you'll do. Keep it short so people actually read it. I don't know where I got it from. It feels like something you'd do. The sleeve's off. The skin's pink and shiny and Malik says my arm looks like a pear. Ribs are fine. Mom's watch is on my wrist, still on Aurora time, so I know it's five in the morning there and you're watching this with the coffee maker going. Mine says 259. Okonkwo's says 266, which is the board's. Arrival's day 268. Same minus nine. Their minus two. The other place is coming along. Still not in my number. Tell Quinn I said hi. I've never met her and I feel like I have. Log fifty four. Ada out.

He played the two entries again. Then he got up and went to the shelf where he kept Ruth's pages in a manila folder, and took out page one, and laid it on the table beside the tablet, and looked from one to the other. A date. What happened. What you'd do. Capitals. Ada had never seen a page of Ruth's in her life.

At nine, at Watkins, the program's own lessons learned register had three hundred and forty two entries in it. Quinn had kept it since March of last year, started the week the plan was baselined, and most of it was good and none of it had left the building. The ARA's closeout instructions said lessons were due ninety days after the end of the mission.

Two of the entries were new, from Wendell's sessions. The ARA's standard test procedure for crit 1 valves didn't ask anyone to record the thermal state of the valve on a repro attempt. And it didn't ask anyone to record the accelerometer channel, only to listen to it, so the knock and the shoulder Wendell had heard since the Petrel had never once been kept.

Quinn finds the owners by Wednesday: the ARA's test standards office owns the crit 1 valve procedure. Sam sends the two entries with the evidence, Wendell's name beside each, and a sentence asking for a change. The office calls on Thursday. Both changes go into the next revision: record the frost line and the flange temperature on every repro attempt, and record the accelerometer channel on every crit 1 valve test. The ARA's next crit 1 valve test, a cargo lander's in March, will be the first to use them. The register goes on the agenda of the Monday program meeting, ten minutes, two entries a week, to a named owner. On Tuesday night Sam asks Ada, in his reply, whether her station's lessons could go into the register. Not her log. Her lessons. She answers in a packet note the next afternoon, and sends twelve.

Wednesday, December 13. 9:00 AM. The last ground run of the workaround campaign, cycles thirty one to forty, after the longest soak yet. The board's data closed at five that afternoon, for the session in the morning.
Arlo had the console, signed off that morning in ink, at the bench, before the run. Wendell had the chair beside it, and the headset.

Wendell's contract ended on Friday, the day after the board. He'd picked it himself. The board's docket notice for the 14th had asked for the test conductor of record to attend, and Wendell said he'd go to that and then he'd go home.

Tallgrass's communications office wanted an event. Garrett's office had ordered a plaque, with a pronghorn on it, and asked Greaves's producers whether they'd like to film the presentation at the Friday all hands, which they would. Corinne had a checklist: his badge, his tools, the stand's records, the console log, his contract, his last timesheet. Hana had written something on a card and hadn't given it to anybody.
Wendell, asked by Quinn on Monday what he'd like, had said he'd like to go home with his thermos.

He wants the last run with Arlo in the chair and himself beside it, and coffee from the thermos after, in the blockhouse, with whoever's on shift. So that's what it is. Cycle thirty three has a ripple on it and Arlo says there before it's over, and Wendell says, Yep, and nothing else. Afterward Corinne walks the checklist with him at the bench, and he hands over the badge himself, and the stand's records go into the archive with his name on the cover sheet as test conductor of record, 2059 to 2062. Hana gives him her card. Sam gives him a letter that says what he did, by date: the third attempt he asked for in September 2059, the notebooks he carried into Room 4, the night shifts of this autumn, the shoulder and the frost, written into a procedure with his name on it. Garrett's plaque goes to Byers in the mail. Wendell puts it in the truck, face down, next to the shoebox.

Wednesday, December 13. 11:30 PM. The kitchen in Aurora. He'd come home at eight and eaten standing up, and then sat down at the table with Ruth's twelve pages in their folder and the tablet beside them, and hadn't opened either.

The last run had ended at 1:50 PM, inside Wendell's five hours. Cycle thirty three had had its ripple, and Arlo had said there before it was over, and Wendell had said yep. Afterward there'd been coffee from the thermos in the blockhouse, in paper cups, for nine people, which was more than the thermos held, and somehow it had held it.

Ilse Brandvold's kneeboard card was in Sam's inbox, photographed, because she'd wanted him to see it. Eleven lines in her handwriting, the first one in Wendell's capitals, copied exactly: IF POSITION WIGGLES AND PRESSURE DOESN'T, BELIEVE THE PRESSURE. The crew would carry it to orbit on January 9 and to Mars after that. The shoulder and the frost weren't in one head anymore. They were in theirs, and Arlo's, and Quinn's, and that was the point.

Arlo's sign off sheet was in the file, pencil and then ink. Trace eleven was taped to the blockhouse wall above the coffee can, with a line under it in Arlo's writing: CAMERA OUT, DON'T CALL IT. Ada's twelve lessons had come up in that afternoon's packet note, and they were in the register under her own name, with the confession book's two entries on top.

Five weeks of handing things to other people. Most of it, he thought, had landed where it was supposed to. He'd been a crew chief long enough to know that a hand off you feel good about is the one you check twice.
At 11:40 the tablet chimed the plain chime it used for work. The board's docket system had run its batch.

INDEPENDENT READINESS BOARD DOCKET SESSION OF THURSDAY, DECEMBER 14, 2062, 0900. ITEM 1. CR 62-311: CHOICE OF RESPONSE FOR I-62-117 (HALCYON MOIV-1). WORKAROUND, OR REPLACEMENT BY SPACEWALK.. MEMBERS SITTING: THE CHAIR. R. CALDER. FOUR OTHERS.. THE BOARD REQUESTS THAT THE TEST CONDUCTOR OF RECORD AND HIS SUCCESSOR ATTEND IN PERSON.. SUBMISSIONS: PROGRAM DATA PACKAGE, CLOSED 1700 WED DEC 13. TALLGRASS AEROSPACE: REQUEST FOR WAIVER 62-14, FILED 1812 WED DEC 13.. CLERK OF THE BOARD
He hadn't filed a waiver. He opened it.

REQUEST FOR WAIVER 62-14 CRITICALITY 1 ITEM OPEN AT FLIGHT READINESS. ITEM: I-62-117 AR 2207. MOIV-1, HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE.. REQUEST: FLY MOIV-1 WITH THE CR 62-311 WORKAROUND. ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION TO CONTINUE DURING CRUISE. REPLACEMENT BY SPACEWALK NOT REQUIRED.. RATIONALE: GROUND RUNS WITH THE WORKAROUND NOMINAL. THE PROGRAM JUDGES THE RISK ACCEPTABLE.. PREPARED BY: OFFICE OF THE CHIEF EXECUTIVE, TALLGRASS AEROSPACE.. SIGNATURE: BLANK. S. OKAFOR, PROGRAM MANAGER

His name was typed under the line, in the board's capitals, the way the board wrote everybody's. The word nominal sat in the rationale like it had been there all along. Ruth would read it on the bench at nine, with a green pen. Wendell would be sitting in the second row, with her page in his shirt pocket, and the frost and the knock he'd taught them to watch for were all through the runs it called nominal.
At 11:52 Garrett texted. Sign it in the morning. Board will land there anyway. This just makes it ours.

Sam put the tablet face down on the table. On the counter by the door, under his keys, the envelope he'd addressed to Ruth in February was where it had been since, with the photocopy in it, still unsealed. He didn't open that either.
Over the high bay doors, twenty miles east, the clock was about to say 66.
